title: AI Fashion Photography vs. a Traditional Photoshoot: Which Shots Do You Need?
metaTitle: AI Fashion Photography vs. Traditional Photoshoots | SetlesStudio
excerpt: Which shots can you make from a flat lay, and when do you need the garment on a person? Use this shot list to plan your next clothing launch.
metaDescription: Compare AI and traditional fashion photography shot by shot. See a real outfit example and learn when to book a model, shoot a detail or use AI.
body: Look at the little bow on the burgundy top in our flat lay. Pulling that tie gathers the fabric at one hip and lifts the hem above the white skirt. A shopper might want to know two things about it. What would this top look like with a skirt? How much shorter does it get when I pull the tie? An AI fashion photo can illustrate the outfit. For the second question, put the sample on a person and photograph the tie loose and cinched. That distinction can save you from booking an entire shoot when you need three frames. It can also tell you when booking the shoot is worth every dollar. ## Which method belongs on your shot list? | What the shopper needs to see | What to commission | What to check before approval | | --- | --- | --- | | An outfit idea for a collection launch | An AI on-model image from an approved product reference | Can you trace the neckline, side tie and hem back to the original? | | Where the skirt lands on a particular size | A traditional fitting photo of the sample | Record the model’s height and the sample size alongside the shot. | | How the pleats open when someone walks | A short video of someone walking in the garment | Include the turn and a moment standing still so the viewer can compare. | | A second setting for an existing campaign | An AI lifestyle variation of the approved look | Check the garment against the reference again under the new lighting. | | The surface of a fabric or finish of a clasp | A close-up of the actual product | Check the full-resolution image against the sample before cropping. | ## What one SetlesStudio outfit can tell you Our starting image shows a sleeveless burgundy top, a white pleated skirt and a quilted bag arranged on a pale background. In one studio version, the model holds the bag by its chain, down beside the skirt. You can follow the curve of the top’s hem all the way to the bow. In another, she carries the bag on her shoulder. That small styling change matters. If the listing is for the top, choose the frame where the shopper can see the gathering. If the listing is for the bag, choose the frame that shows its front and add a real close-up of the clasp. The flower-shop version gives the outfit a place to go. It makes sense as the opening image in a spring launch email. For a shopper zooming in to inspect the skirt, I’d use the quieter studio frame and a close-up of the real pleats. You can see the source outfit and the different treatments in our [studio and lifestyle photo example](/blog/ai-fashion-product-photography-studio-or-lifestyle). Here’s the limit of that example. The flat lay shows the tie, but tells us little about how tightly it pulls or how the fabric feels against the skin. Even a convincing on-model image leaves those questions open. If either detail is a selling point, give it a real photo, a measurement or a product description based on the sample. ## Can AI replace your next studio booking? Take the shots from your last launch and mark the ones you could recreate from approved product photos. A different backdrop for the same look is a good candidate. A back view of a jacket when you have only photographed the front leaves the vent, seams and fastening to guesswork. Get a back reference first. If the point of the shot is to show how the vent opens when the wearer sits, book a model and capture that action. Ask both providers to quote the same shot list. Include the number of garments, views, detail crops, revisions and final file sizes. Add sample preparation and product review to the AI quote. Add studio time, styling, retouching and usage rights where applicable to the traditional quote. Compare the cost per image you can actually publish. An inexpensive variation has little value if the merchandiser has to reject it because the pocket moved. ## A one-garment test before you commit the collection 1. Pick a garment with one detail your customers ask about. For our burgundy top, I’d pick the side tie. 2. Photograph that detail and the whole garment in even light. Keep an unedited reference for whoever signs off the work. 3. Commission one on-model front view. Open it beside the source and follow the tie from the gathered seam to the loose ends. Check the same area again at phone size. 4. Write down the decision for that image: approve for the product gallery, use for styling inspiration, or reshoot. Give a specific reason. “The bag covers the bow” is feedback a photographer or an AI artist can use. Planning a launch? Send us a flat lay or product photo, tell us which item you’re selling, and name the detail your customer will zoom in on. We can use that brief to plan your [on-model studio images](/services/realistic-ai-studio-photography) or [lifestyle campaign](/services/lifestyle-realistic-ai-photography).
